file.content: The present disclosure relates to cordless handheld vacuum lifters, and more particularly to a cordless handheld vacuum lifter having a grip-loss warning indicator.

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

27	There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colors which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. The sufficiency indicated in that device is determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source rather than from a measurement of the vacuum holding the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1]. That equipment is frame-mounted rather than hand-carried, its controller cycles the vacuum pump on the pressure data to maintain a partial vacuum at a setpoint vacuum pressure, and the indicators are described as indicating a functional condition of a module rather than as being timed with respect to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the workpiece.

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the person carrying the panel is given no signal that is tied to the vacuum still needed to hold it. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a determination made from the state of the power source, on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the remedies that the known equipment applies to a failing grip are remedies a cordless handheld lifter does not have. A plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 activates while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

That timing answers a technical problem that arises when a suction grip decays in the hand. The decay is progressive and, to the person holding the load, silent: nothing in the feel of the tool changes until the suction cup 10 lets go. A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be answered by running its pump again fixes the value at which it acts by reference to the vacuum it is trying to maintain, and that value says nothing about how much grip is left; when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, the pump runs while the grip continues to decay and the person carrying the load is told nothing. A signal derived instead from the state of the power source, from how fast the vacuum is changing, or from a number that the user must read off a display while carrying a load reports something other than whether the load is about to be released. The activation of the warning indicator 32 is tied to the retention of the load: it occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person whose hand is on the handle 16, and that person can act only if the notice arrives while the suction cup 10 retains the load, with grip remaining to bring the load down.

The pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained on the suction cup 10 and carried by the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is carried by the handle 16.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 creates the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs while the suction cup 10 retains the panel 50, before the panel 50 can be dropped, and while the panel 50 is carried by the handle 16.

file.content: A cordless handheld vacuum lifter has a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip that is placed against a panel of glass or stone. An electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum that retains a load on the suction cup, a pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum, and a rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter creating the grip vacuum, monitoring the grip vacuum, and activating a warning indicator without a cord to an external power supply. The warning indicator, driven by the pressure sensor, activates when the grip vacuum is lost and while the suction cup retains the load, before the load can be dropped.

Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. When the user presses the activation key, the vacuum pump will act to pump out the air between the electric sucker and the component attached to the electric sucker, so that the electric sucker is adsorbed on the component. The pressure sensing unit can detect the pressure between the electric sucker and the component in real time. When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air between the electric suction cup and the component again. After the user sets up the electric chuck on the component that wants to adsorb, can make the electric chuck adsorb automatically on simply through pressing the start key on the component. Then, the electric suction cup can automatically detect the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component in real time, and automatically perform air suction again when the pressure is lower than a second preset pressure, so that the safety of related personnel using the electric suction cup can be ensured.

A fluid circuit interconnects the vacuum pump with the port. The vacuum pump is operable to draw gas from within the internal region through the fluid circuit to generate a partial vacuum within the internal region and reversibly attach the cup to the workpiece. An interface is configured to communicate with controllers of the vacuum modules. A user selects an operational mode of the vacuum modules; the state of the controllers is dependent on the selected operational mode.

Each cup has a body, a rim to contact a workpiece, an internal region defined by the body and bounded by the rim, and a port that extends through the body and opens into the internal region. content.text:
I've read the sources, the full draft, every figure brief, and all ten prior-art files. Here's what I found.

**Workspace state:** `figures/` contains only the three Markdown briefs — there are no `rendered-*.png` files, and `review/figure-audit-evidence.json` does not exist, so no pixel-level verification was possible. Both mechanical failures trace to that single root cause: the three briefs between them do assign all 16 numerals in `numerals.md`, so nothing needs to be added to or removed from the briefs or the text.

**Source fidelity:** every claim limitation, numeral, part, relationship and figure-brief element traces to the inventor's disclosure. Claim 1 recasts the inventor's own claims 1+2 ("activate when the vacuum is lost" + "before a load can be dropped"); claims 2–4 and 6–8 recast the disclosed cordless attribute, the handheld carrying function, and "for glass and stone panels." No threshold, modality, dimension, material or sensor-plumbing detail was invented, and none of the FIG. 4 / three-vacuum-level material described in the drafter's turn survives in the current text. The two minor findings from the previous QA round (causal "such that" for cordless operation, and the "grips/monitors/warns" vocabulary split) are both fixed.

**Citations:** all ten `[REF:]` characterisations check out against the actual reference files — including the US-10625955-B2 high/low predetermined pressure pair, the US-10518985-B2 rate-of-change warning (claims 3–4), the WO-2017156581-A1 attach indicator (claim 6), the US-5374090-A voltage-drop LED determination (claim 2), and the WO-2022236379-A1 frame-mounted modules. One uncited generalisation in the detailed description does not match the record, noted below.

input.summary: The draft is faithful to the inventor's disclosure and honest in its citations. I built a full source ledger: every claim limitation, every one of the 16 numerals, and every structure, relationship and figure-brief element traces to an affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md (reproduced verbatim as the first USER turn of input/conversation.md) — the nine inventor numerals are used exactly as assigned, and the seven drafter numerals (40 is the inventor's; 50, 100, 202, 204, 205, 206, 208 are the drafter's) name only parts and steps the inventor described. Claim 1 combines the inventor's own claims 1 and 2; claims 2-8 recast only disclosed functions. No threshold, modality, dimension, material, rated-load or sensor-plumbing detail was invented, and no FIG. 4 / three-vacuum-level material from the earlier drafting turn survives. All ten [REF:] characterisations in the Background are supported by the corresponding prior_art/ files, checked passage by passage. The two minor findings of the previous QA round are fixed. Terminology is consistent (grip vacuum, warning indicator, rigid body) between claims, summary, description and abstract; the abstract is 134 words. The decisive defect is completeness of the drawing package: the specification describes FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, and briefs exist for all three, but figures/ contains no rendered image at all and review/figure-audit-evidence.json is absent, so no visible geometry, leader or numeral could be verified. Two smaller items: an uncited prior-art generalisation in the detailed description ("equipment that hangs from a frame") that no cited reference supports and that departs from the Background's own accurate wording, and mixed first-mention article usage in the detailed description.

findings.title: No drawing sheet exists for any described figure; every specification numeral is therefore absent from the drawings
findings.where: figures/ (whole directory) against draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md
findings.detail: draft/07-drawings.md describes three figures and draft/08-detailed-description.md states what each of them shows, but figures/ contains only the three Markdown briefs (FIG-1-SIDE-ELEVATION-OF-THE-LIFTER.md, FIG-2-SCHEMATIC-DIAGRAM-OF-THE-LIFTER.md, FIG-3-FLOW-DIAGRAM-OF-THE-METHOD-OF-LIFTING-A-PANEL.md). There is no rendered-*.png file for any of them, and review/ contains only previous-qa.md, with no figure-audit-evidence.json. Because no sheet exists, all 16 reference numerals defined in draft/numerals.md and used in the specification (10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22, 30, 32, 40, 50, 100, 202, 204, 205, 206, 208) appear in no drawing, which is exactly what both mechanical checks report. This is a completeness defect in the package rather than a defect in the briefs: the three briefs are internally consistent with the text and between them assign every numeral (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 50, 100; FIG. 2: 10, 20, 22, 30, 32, 40; FIG. 3: 202, 204, 205, 206, 208), each brief's numeral list matches the Brief Description and the detailed description, and no numeral labels two different parts. No sheet contains a section line, so no section-designation or hatch check arises. I could not verify any visible geometry, leader path or printed numeral, because there are no pixels to open.
findings.evidence: draft/07-drawings.md: "FIG. 1 is a side elevation view of a cordless handheld vacuum lifter according to an embodiment, shown with the flexible sealing lip seated against a panel and with the electric vacuum pump shown in broken lines within the rigid body." / "FIG. 2 is a schematic diagram of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter of FIG. 1..." / "FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel using the cordless handheld vacuum lifter of FIG. 1." -- while `ls figures/` returns only FIG-1-SIDE-ELEVATION-OF-THE-LIFTER.md, FIG-2-SCHEMATIC-DIAGRAM-OF-THE-LIFTER.md and FIG-3-FLOW-DIAGRAM-OF-THE-METHOD-OF-LIFTING-A-PANEL.md.
findings.fix: Render one sheet per existing brief, exactly as each brief specifies, and place them in figures/ as rendered-FIG-1-..., rendered-FIG-2-... and rendered-FIG-3-.... FIG. 1 carries 10, 12, 14, 16, 20 (broken-line rectangle wholly inside the outline of 14), 50 and 100 (led to the outline of the assembly as a whole); FIG. 2 carries 10, 20, 22, 30, 32 and 40, one numeral led well inside each of the six rectangles, with the arrowhead at 32 on the line from 30; FIG. 3 carries 202, 204, 205, 206 and 208 in a single top-to-bottom column of five rectangles joined by downward flow arrows. That covers all 16 numerals and requires no change to draft/07-drawings.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, draft/numerals.md or any brief.

findings.title: The detailed description attributes two prior-art remedies to equipment "that hangs from a frame", which no cited reference supports and which departs from the Background's own accurate wording
findings.where: draft/08-detailed-description.md, paragraph beginning "The distinction does real work on a tool that is carried in the hand" (line 13)
findings.detail: The sentence asserts a fact about known equipment. The two remedies it names trace to prior_art/US-5310232-A.md ("a battery-fed emergency vacuum source is provided which can be started by an emergency switch") and prior_art/US-10518985-B2.md ("limit or alter machine functions to reduce risk exposure"), and the Background states both accurately and with citations: "A plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]." Neither file describes its device as hanging from a frame: US-5310232-A is a suction plate assembly / vacuum vessel, and US-10518985-B2 is a control system for a vacuum attachment apparatus. The only frame-mounted reference in prior_art/ is WO-2022236379-A1, and the draft itself says that its response is different ("its controller cycles the vacuum pump on the pressure data to maintain a partial vacuum at a setpoint vacuum pressure"). So the description generalises the two remedies onto a class of equipment the record does not tie them to, and says something narrower-but-different from the Background about the same art.
findings.evidence: draft/08-detailed-description.md: "Vacuum handling equipment that hangs from a frame can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source or by refusing to move. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it."
findings.fix: Conform the sentence to the Background's supported wording by removing the frame attribution: "Vacuum handling equipment that is not carried in the hand can answer a failing grip with a further vacuum source, or by limiting or altering machine functions. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has no such remedy available to it." Nothing else in the paragraph needs to change.

findings.title: Mixed first-mention articles in the detailed description, including one element introduced with "The" before it is introduced at all
findings.detail: The electric vacuum pump 20 and the port 22 make their first appearance in the detailed description with the definite article, while the pressure sensor 30, warning indicator 32 and rechargeable battery 40 are introduced with the indefinite article in the very next sentence, so the same list mixes both forms. The summary already uses the correct form ("An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port"). This is a wording formality only; every element involved is disclosed and none of the substance changes.
findings.evidence: draft/08-detailed-description.md: "The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1." and "FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them."
findings.fix: Introduce each element once with the indefinite article and use the definite article thereafter: change the first sentence to "An electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1." and the second to "FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, a port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them." All later occurrences already read "the ..." and need no change.

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried powered suction devices have likewise been described. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, a switch by which the pump is turned on and off, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, the sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across a resistor network fed by the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated there is the state of the power source and the sufficiency of the suction force for taking hold, not how much hold remains on an object already being carried.
12	
13	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed to the upper end of a suction cup body and a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, with a control unit connected between the pump and the power supply part, so that air is pumped out from between the suction cup body and the surface of a smooth material and is continuously pumped out after an airtight state has been reached in order to avoid loosening and falling during movement; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change, with a light source displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. Here again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep the pump running, and what the buzzer is tied to is a usage state rather than the amount of grip left.
14	
15	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure carrying a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure carrying a battery and an electric vacuum pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, and the lower part of the battery end carrying an air pressure sensor and a display screen which displays the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power, the battery being charged through a USB charging port [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device puts a number in front of the user and leaves the reading of the number, and the judgement of what it means for the panel in hand, to the user.
16	
17	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating a suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, a power storage unit, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, together with an attach indicator which the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator there reports that attachment has been achieved, being activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, and the response to a vacuum level below the preselected minimum is once more to run the pump.
18	
19	A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not describe in terms of the degree of vacuum below which the sucker would let go of the plate it is carrying.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
26

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, the handle 16, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, and a rechargeable battery 40.
6	
7	The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects away from the rigid body 14. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. The rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand.
12	
13	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32. All of these parts are carried by the rigid body 14, and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use.
14	
15	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.
16	
17	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, which is the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The release vacuum is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and attitude in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The other is the warning vacuum, which is the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate, and which is a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100.
18	
19	The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.
20	
21	This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is fixed by reference to the vacuum at which the lifter is fit to lift: it is placed a little below that vacuum so that the grip is topped up often and the pump cycles little. Such a value says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.
22	
23	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
24	
25	In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 activates at the warning vacuum whether or not the electric vacuum pump 20 is operating. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the vacuum falls to the warning vacuum while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.
26	
27	In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to conform to and seal against the face of a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the vacuum. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: panels of this kind are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.
28	
29	In embodiments, the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 close to the port 22, so that the volume from which air is drawn is short and small. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described above, because a leak of a given size then produces a fall in the vacuum that is prompt enough to be monitored by the pressure sensor 30 rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.
30	
31	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.
32	
33	At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained, the rechargeable battery 40 powering the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 throughout. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 still retains the load, using the reserve of grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.
34	
35	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

The lifter of claim 8, wherein: a) said valve assembly includes a three way valve and a check valve. The lifter of claim 7, wherein: a) said applying means includes a through pipe extending through said vessel and communicating with said chamber; and b) a vacuum pipe extends from the interior of said vessel and communicates with said through pipe. The lifter in claim 7, wherein: a) a central pipe extends between said plates; and b) an aperture in said bottom plate is aligned with said central pipe so that said central pipe is open to the atmosphere. A vacuum lifter, comprising: a) a vacuum vessel comprising upper and lower plates and a peripheral wall extending therebetween; b) at least first and second resilient seals extending from and about said lower plate for defining therebetween a vacuum chamber; c) a main vacuum source and an emergency vacuum source, each of said sources communicating with the interior of said vessel for applying a vacuum thereto, wherein said emergency vacuum source is electrically operable during application of the vacuum thereof; d) a measurement pick-up operatively associated with said vessel for monitoring the vacuum therein; e) a vacuum supply extending between said vessel and said chamber for causing the vacuum inside said vessel to be selectively applied to said chamber; and f) control means operatively associated with said emergency vacuum source and said pick-up for causing automatic electrical operation of said emergency vacuum source when said monitoring means detects in said vacuum chamber a vacuum pressure less than a preselected limit. The lifter of claim 12, wherein said vacuum supply system includes: a) an aperture in said upper plate; b) a through pipe extending through said vessel and communicating with said chamber; and c) a vacuum pipe interconnecting said aperture and said through pipe. The lifter of claim 13, wherein: a) a valve assembly is interposed in said vacuum pipe for permitting said through pipe and thereby said chamber to vent to atmosphere while maintaining the vacuum in said vessel. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) said control means includes a remotely operable switch for causing operation of said emergency vacuum source. The lifter of claim 15, wherein: a) said switch is operable when the vacuum in said vessel is less than said preselected limit so that said main and emergency vacuum sources may operate simultaneously. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) said emergency vacuum source includes an electrically operable motor; and b) a battery is operably associated with said motor for assuring operation thereof. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) each of said seals is resilient.

13	Abstract: A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers during the manufacture of integrated circuits. The wand device comprises a housing having a hollow interior and a tip for grasping objects. The tip is attached to the housing through a hollow tube, and has a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of an object to be grasped. The tip also has a recessed interior region having an air inlet therein. The wand device includes a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing. The vacuum pump produces a suction force at the air inlet on the tip. When the tip is placed against the surface of an object, the object is securely grasped due to the suction force exerted thereon by the wand tip. A switch located on the wand may be used to turn the vacuum pump on or off in order to grasp or release the object. Light-emitting diodes of different colors indicate to an operator whether or not the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object.
14	Claims: A cordless apparatus for grasping objects said apparatus comprising: a cordless housing having a first air inlet therein; means within said housing for creating a suction force at said first air inlet; means for applying said suction force to a surface of object to be grasped; and means for indicating to an operator whether said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object, said indicating means comprising: a first light-emitting diode which illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object; a second light-emitting diode which illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is not of sufficient strength to grasp said object; and means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force. The apparatus of claim 1 wherein the means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force includes: a power source disposed within said apparatus, said power source having a positive pole and a negative pole; a first resistor electrically connected between said positive pole of said power source and electrical ground; a second resistor connected in series with said first resistor; a third resistor connected in series with said first and second resistors; and an integrated circuit connected in parallel with said first, second, and third resistors, said integrated circuit detecting the voltage drop across each of said resistors, and causing said first light-emitting diode to illuminate when the total voltage drop exceeds a predetermined threshold, and causing said second light-emitting diode to illuminate when said total voltage drop is less than said predetermined threshold. Warnings are engaged if parameters or limits are not met. At designated/calculated thresholds and conditions the device can adjust its utilization of resources to ensure the safest condition. If conditions are detected that indicate a reduced ability to maintain the attachment, the programmable controller may limit functions such as preventing the operator from initiating another attachment.

The system of claim 1 , wherein said apparatus limits a said level of vacuum in said vacuum circuit so as to prevent damaging the attachment surface. The system of claim 1 , wherein said electronic controller is configured to process one or more algorithms that evaluate a change in said received measured vacuum level values over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak. The system of claim 3 wherein, when said rate of said vacuum level change exceeds a threshold rate, a warning indication is output to alert an operator. The system of claim 1 , wherein said electronic controller is configured to determine whether a load is attached to said vacuum attachment apparatus, wherein said determination comprises a finding that at least one measured vacuum level values from said vacuum level sensing circuit indicates at least one of (i) a higher level of vacuum than would be expected when said vacuum attachment apparatus is unattached, (ii) a higher level of vacuum than would be expected when said vacuum attachment apparatus was unattached and maintained for a period of time, and (iii) a pattern of change of said level of vacuum that would not be expected when said vacuum attachment apparatus is unattached. The system of claim 1 , wherein said vacuum attachment apparatus incorporates an attach mode in which the system takes actions in order to obtain and sustain a sufficient level of vacuum to maintain an attachment to said surface wherein, as the system operates said vacuum attachment apparatus, said electronic controller stores in memory an indication of whether or not the system is in said attach mode and wherein, upon a power-up of the system, said stored indication is read to determine if the system was in said attach mode when power was last lost and, when said indication is indicative of being in said attach mode when power was last lost, said programmed controller operates said system to restore the system to the said attach mode. The system of claim 1 , wherein said vacuum attachment apparatus incorporates an attach mode in which the system takes actions in order to obtain and sustain a sufficient level of vacuum to maintain an attachment to said surface, wherein during operation of said vacuum attachment apparatus, said electronic controller is configured to make a determination whether said system is in said attach mode, and wherein said electronic controller is configured to change or delay the process used to shut down said system when it is determined that said system is in said attach mode.
