content.text: I have read every source, draft section, figure brief and prior-art file. Here is what I found.

input.summary:
The candidate is a well-organised, internally coherent application whose prior-art discussion is, with two exceptions, faithful to the files in prior_art/ (US-10625955-B2, CN-110630621-B, US-10518985-B2, US-5310232-A, US-5374090-A, CN-2806399-Y, US-2024424646-A1, WO-2017156581-A1, WO-2022236379-A1 all check out against their quoted claims/abstracts). Its central recited relationship — the warning indicator activating at a warning vacuum reached before a release vacuum at which the cup ceases to retain the load — is a fair restatement in vacuum terms of the inventor's "The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped."

The problem is everything built around that core. The inventor's disclosure is nine sentences long and places only three things: the pump inside the rigid body, the lip on the cup, the handle on the body. The candidate nevertheless recites, in independent and dependent claims and supports in its own detailed description, a set of structures, placements, power connections and functional relationships the disclosure never states: pump-independent activation, the pump located close to the port with a consequently small evacuated volume, the indicator carried by and positioned on the rigid body, the battery powering the sensor and the indicator, and operation "without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body" — the last taken almost verbatim from the search wording in input/request.md, which expressly told the drafter to treat it "as a pointer to look in input/disclosure.md, never as text to import." The FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs add exactly the two artefacts input/request.md named as previously rejected: a duct between port and pump, and a sensing branch to the pressure sensor, together with a sensing location for the pressure sensor. Under the source-ledger rule these are all critical.

Note on scope of the figure review: figures/ contains only the four Markdown briefs. There are no rendered-*.png files and no review/figure-audit-evidence.json in this workspace, so no pixel, OCR, leader, hatch or cutting-plane verification was possible; the two mechanical failures you supplied are consistent with that. My figure findings are therefore against the brief text only, and I make no claim about rendered geometry.

findings.title: Pump-independent activation of the warning indicator is not in the inventor's disclosure
findings.detail: Three claims and two specification paragraphs recite that the indicator fires irrespective of whether the pump is running, and that it fires while the pump is still drawing air and losing ground to a leak. The inventor's disclosure says nothing whatever about the state of the pump at the moment of warning; it says only that the pump draws air through a port and that the indicator activates when vacuum is lost. This is an added functional relationship, and it is the relationship the conversation record shows the drafter selected as the sharpest distinction over the restart-threshold references — which is precisely why it needs a source and does not have one. The candidate's own detailed description cannot supply the support, because the candidate wrote it.
findings.evidence: Claim 2: "wherein the warning indicator is configured to activate at the warning vacuum whether or not the electric vacuum pump is operating." Claim 3: "...while the electric vacuum pump continues to draw air through the port and the vacuum continues to be lost." Detailed description ¶25: "If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the vacuum falls to the warning vacuum while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up." The whole of input/disclosure.md on the pump and the indicator is: "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum... The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: Cancel claims 2, 3 and 10 and renumber. Delete detailed-description ¶25 in full and delete the sentence in the summary beginning "In embodiments, the warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost whether or not the electric vacuum pump is running...". No other passage depends on them.

findings.title: Claim 8 and its supporting paragraph add a pump-to-port proximity, a small evacuated volume, and a resulting measurement behaviour
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that the pump is disposed inside the rigid body and draws air through a port. The candidate adds a positional relationship (pump close to the port), a consequent geometric property (the evacuated volume is short and small), and a consequent measurement result (a leak produces a fall prompt enough to be monitored rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir). Position, volume and the asserted sensing consequence are each untraced; the reservoir comparison is an engineering result the inventor never reports.
findings.evidence: Claim 8: "wherein the electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body close to the port, such that a volume from which air is drawn is short and small and a leak produces a fall in the vacuum that is monitored by the pressure sensor." Detailed description ¶29: "A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described above, because a leak of a given size then produces a fall in the vacuum that is prompt enough to be monitored by the pressure sensor 30 rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir." input/disclosure.md says only: "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum."
findings.fix: Cancel claim 8 and renumber. Delete detailed-description ¶29 in full. The disclosed relationship ("disposed within the rigid body") already appears in claim 1 and in ¶9 and is unaffected.

findings.title: "Without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body" is imported search wording, not inventor disclosure
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 4 and 12; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3 and ¶13; draft/06-summary.md ¶11
findings.detail: The inventor discloses a "cordless handheld vacuum lifter" and nothing more about external connections. The candidate converts that adjective into a recited negative limitation excluding a hose, a cord and an external controller, and asserts it four times. The wording tracks the search phrase quoted in input/request.md, which the drafter was told in terms not to import: "They are quoted in the SEARCH's words, not the inventor's: treat each as a pointer to look in input/disclosure.md, never as text to import." A hose exclusion and an external-controller exclusion are separate technical assertions from cordlessness and neither is disclosed.
findings.evidence: Claim 4: "...such that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter creates the vacuum, monitors the vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body." Claim 12: "...carrying the load with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body." Detailed description ¶3: "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14." input/request.md: "single-hand portable design with all components carried by rigid body without external hose or cord" ... "never as text to import." input/disclosure.md contains no reference to a hose, a cord or a controller.
findings.fix: Cancel claims 4 and 12 and renumber. In ¶3 delete the sentence beginning "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit..."; in ¶13 delete the final clause "and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use"; delete summary ¶11. The disclosed word "cordless" remains in the title, field and every claim preamble.

findings.title: The warning indicator's mounting and viewing position are recited and drawn but never disclosed
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 6 and 9; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶11; draft/06-summary.md ¶3 and ¶9; figures/FIG-1-SIDE-ELEVATION-LIFTER-IN-USE.md
findings.detail: The disclosure locates the pump ("inside the rigid body 14"), the lip (on the cup) and the handle (on the body), and locates nothing else. It never says the warning indicator is on or carried by the rigid body, still less that it is placed where a user gripping the handle can perceive it. "Carried by the rigid body" appears in independent claims 1 and 9, and the perceptibility limitation is claim 6. The FIG. 1 brief then fixes the placement on the sheet, which is geometry the text was widened to legitimise rather than the other way round.
findings.evidence: Claim 1: "a warning indicator carried by the rigid body and driven by the pressure sensor". Claim 6: "wherein the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle." Detailed description ¶11: "The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool." FIG. 1 brief: "The warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small discrete element on the outer surface of the upper side of the rigid body 14, beside the handle 16, facing upward toward the user." input/disclosure.md: "The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: In claims 1 and 9 delete "carried by the rigid body and" / "a warning indicator carried by the rigid body" so the indicator is recited exactly as disclosed ("a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor"). Cancel claim 6 and renumber. In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14..."; delete the corresponding sentence in summary ¶9 and the words "carried by the rigid body and" in summary ¶3. In the FIG. 1 brief, either drop 32 from the sheet or reduce the entry to "the warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small plain outline on the rigid body 14" with no facing, side or beside-the-handle statement.

findings.title: The battery is claimed as carried by the rigid body and as powering the pressure sensor and the warning indicator; the disclosure says only that it powers the pump
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 5, 9 and 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶11 and ¶33; draft/06-summary.md ¶3
findings.detail: The single disclosed sentence about the battery is "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." The candidate adds two things: a mounting ("carried by the rigid body", in both independent claims) and two further power connections to the sensor and the indicator, together with the consequence that monitoring and warning are available whenever the tool is in hand. Claims 5 and 14 recite the added connections outright.
findings.evidence: Claim 1: "a rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body and configured to power the electric vacuum pump." Claim 5: "wherein the rechargeable battery is further configured to power the pressure sensor and the warning indicator." Claim 14: "further comprising powering the pressure sensor and the warning indicator from the rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body while the load is retained." Detailed description ¶11: "The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand." input/disclosure.md: "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20."
findings.fix: Cancel claims 5 and 14 and renumber. In claims 1 and 9 delete "carried by the rigid body and" before "configured to power the electric vacuum pump". In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30..." and in ¶13 delete ", the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32" so the sentence reads "The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." In ¶33 delete ", the rechargeable battery 40 powering the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 throughout". In summary ¶3 delete "carried by the rigid body". Correspondingly delete the battery-to-sensor/indicator power lines from the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs.

findings.title: FIG. 2 brief invents a duct between port and pump and a sensing location for the pressure sensor
findings.detail: The brief specifies a short duct with hatched walls running from the port to the pump, a flow arrow inside it, a path from beneath the cup into the body interior, and — most seriously — places the pressure sensor adjacent that duct. Where the sensor is plumbed is nowhere in the inventor's disclosure, which says only "A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum." input/request.md records this exact class of addition as having sunk an earlier round ("new structure: a suction passage, a sensing branch, a sealed region, each given a numeral and a location nobody disclosed") and imposes a hard rule against it: "introduce NO new numbered part, passage, region, port, chamber, surface or other structure". Being unnumbered does not make the duct any less a new passage, and the sensor's position beside it asserts a sensing point on the drawing.
findings.evidence: FIG. 2 brief: "The electric vacuum pump 20 is a block inside the interior cavity, on one side of the vertical centre line, positioned close to the port 22 and connected to it by a short duct drawn as a pair of hatched walls. An arrow inside that duct points from the port 22 toward the electric vacuum pump 20 to show the direction of air flow. The pressure sensor 30 is a smaller block inside the interior cavity, adjacent the duct between the port 22 and the electric vacuum pump 20." Also: "The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening through the wall of the suction cup 10 on the vertical centre line, giving a path from beneath the suction cup 10 into the interior of the rigid body 14."
findings.fix: Rewrite these three bullets to the disclosed facts only: "The electric vacuum pump 20 is a plain block inside the interior cavity of the rigid body 14. The pressure sensor 30 is a smaller plain block inside the interior cavity. The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening on the vertical centre line through which the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air." Delete the duct, its hatched walls, the flow arrow, the "positioned close to the port 22" phrase, the "path... into the interior of the rigid body 14" phrase and the "adjacent the duct" placement.

findings.title: FIG. 3 brief invents a pneumatic sensing branch to the pressure sensor
findings.detail: The schematic routes a branch of the port-to-pump pneumatic line to the pressure sensor block. That branch is a pneumatic connection and a sensing location, neither of which the inventor disclosed; the disclosure states only that the sensor monitors the grip vacuum and drives the indicator. This is the second of the two artefacts input/request.md names by name ("a sensing branch") as having caused an earlier round to be rejected.
findings.evidence: FIG. 3 brief: "The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening through the wall of the suction cup 10 and is connected by a plain pneumatic line running upward into the broken-line rectangle to the block of the electric vacuum pump 20... A branch of that pneumatic line runs to the block of the pressure sensor 30." input/disclosure.md: "A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum. The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: Delete the bullet "A branch of that pneumatic line runs to the block of the pressure sensor 30." Show the pressure sensor 30 as a plain block whose only drawn connection is the signal line to the warning indicator 32, which is the relationship the disclosure states.

findings.title: The sealing lip is given a peripheral position and a projecting form the disclosure does not state
findings.detail: The disclosure says only that the suction cup carries a flexible sealing lip. The candidate adds that the lip runs around the periphery of the cup, that it projects away from the rigid body, that it deflects and conforms on contact, and that it is the only part that touches the workpiece in normal use. Peripheral location and projection direction are structure; "the part... that touches the workpiece" is an exclusivity assertion. The figure briefs then place the lip "at the lower periphery of the suction cup 10" consistently with the added text.
findings.evidence: Detailed description ¶7: "The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects away from the rigid body 14. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use..." input/disclosure.md: "The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14."
findings.fix: Replace ¶7 with the disclosed statement and its immediate function: "The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face." In the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 briefs replace "at the lower periphery of the suction cup 10" with "on the suction cup 10, shown in contact with the upper face of the panel".

findings.title: Asserted facts about glass and stone panels (weight, carrying attitude, shear and tension loading, breakage) have no source
findings.detail: The inventor's only statement about the workpiece is that the lifter is "for glass and stone panels". The candidate adds that such panels are heavy, that they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude, that in that attitude the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and that they break when dropped. The shear/tension loading statement in particular is a mechanical characterisation of the grip that the disclosure does not make, and it is offered as a reason the invention is needed.
findings.evidence: Detailed description ¶27: "panels of this kind are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped." input/disclosure.md: "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels is disclosed."
findings.fix: Delete the clause beginning "panels of this kind are heavy..." to the end of ¶27, leaving "Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended." That sentence traces to "for glass and stone panels".

findings.title: The release vacuum is defined as a property of the load and the warning vacuum as a device setting; neither definition is in the disclosure
findings.detail: The recited relationship — indicator activates before the cup lets go — restates the inventor's "warn a user before a load can be dropped" and is supportable. What is not supportable is the definitional apparatus the candidate builds around it: that the release vacuum is a property of the particular combination of cup, workpiece, load and attitude and is not a device setting, and that the warning vacuum is a setting of the lifter. Those are the kind of new definition and reference point that input/request.md forbids ("no new definition, sign convention, reference point or operating equivalence"). The same paragraph group adds an unsourced use scenario, and claim 11 recites acting on it. I am less sure about claim 11 than about the definitions, since a warning that precedes release implies the user can act; the definitional sentences are the clear additions.
findings.evidence: Detailed description ¶17: "The release vacuum is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and attitude in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The other is the warning vacuum, which is the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate, and which is a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100." ¶19: "...can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack." Claim 11: "further comprising setting the workpiece down while the suction cup is still retaining the load, using grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum." input/disclosure.md says only: "The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped."
findings.fix: In ¶17 delete the two characterising clauses so the paragraph reads: "Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate." In ¶19 delete "and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack" and the parallel sentence in summary ¶5. Amend claim 11 to "further comprising setting the workpiece down while the suction cup is still retaining the load", which tracks the disclosed purpose of the warning without reciting the reserve.

findings.title: The draft asserts how the known restart pressure value is chosen; no cited reference says this
findings.detail: Both passages state as fact that in the known powered devices the low/restart pressure value is fixed by reference to the working vacuum, and the detailed description adds a design rationale ("placed a little below that vacuum so that the grip is topped up often and the pump cycles little"). The two references that disclose a restart value say only that a low predetermined pressure exists and that crossing it restarts the pump; US-10625955-B2 in fact says the high and low predetermined pressures are adjustable from external information, and says nothing about how either is chosen. Neither file states any relationship between the low value and the working vacuum, and no file states the cycling rationale. Characterising the cited art in terms the cited art does not use is the error the Background must not make.
findings.evidence: Background ¶23: "the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left." Detailed description ¶21: "A restart value is fixed by reference to the vacuum at which the lifter is fit to lift: it is placed a little below that vacuum so that the grip is topped up often and the pump cycles little." prior_art/US-10625955-B2.md says only: "when the control unit determines that the pressure of the sealed space is smaller than the low predetermined pressure, the control unit controls the operation of the vacuum pump" and "the control unit is able to receive external information to correspondingly adjust the low predetermined pressure". prior_art/CN-110630621-B.md: "When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air... again."
findings.fix: In Background ¶23 replace the quoted clause with what the files support: "and neither reference relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load." In detailed-description ¶21 replace the first sentence with "A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left", deleting the "fit to lift"/"topped up often"/"cycles little" assertions.

findings.title: Negative characterisation of US-5184858-A is contradicted by the search note in its own prior-art file
findings.detail: The draft's positive recitation of this reference matches its claims and abstract exactly. The trailing negative assertion, however, is contradicted by the "Why the search returned it" note in the same file, which records this reference as the best disclosure found for a warning at a threshold above the release vacuum level, citing paragraph p0003 — a paragraph the file does not quote. I could not resolve the conflict: tools/patent_lookup.py returns "NOT FOUND: US-5184858-A (corpus unavailable)", so the underlying paragraph is unavailable in this workspace. I note that the same note style is demonstrably loose elsewhere (WO-2017156581-A1 carries the identical "best disclosure" label, yet its claim 6 is an attach indicator activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, which the draft characterises correctly). Marking minor because the reference's quoted text supports the draft and only the unquoted search note conflicts.
findings.evidence: Draft ¶19: "the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not describe in terms of the degree of vacuum below which the sucker would let go of the plate it is carrying." prior_art/US-5184858-A.md: "Best disclosure found for: warning indicator remains active while grip vacuum persists below threshold; warning indicator activated when vacuum falls to threshold above release vacuum level (paragraph p0003)." The quoted abstract in the same file says only: "The sound generator is turned on when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum."
findings.fix: Narrow the assertion to what the quoted passages support: "...the sound is generated when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum, the passages of record describing that value only as a predetermined value." This keeps the Background accurate against the file without asserting an absence the file's own note disputes.

findings.title: The workpiece is numbered 50 on FIGS. 1 and 3 but left unnumbered on FIG. 2
findings.detail: FIG. 2 is a section taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, whose cutting plane the FIG. 1 brief runs down past the panel ("its lower physical endpoint is below the workpiece 50"). The same panel therefore appears in FIG. 2, but the brief calls it an unnumbered slab and omits 50 from the figure's numeral list, while FIGS. 1 and 3 both label it 50. The detailed description meanwhile speaks throughout of the lip being placed against the workpiece 50. Labelling the same disclosed part in two views and not the third is a gratuitous inconsistency, and the numeral 50 is already defined in draft/numerals.md.
findings.evidence: FIG. 2 brief: "The flexible sealing lip 12 is at the lower periphery of the suction cup 10 and is shown resting on the upper face of a flat unnumbered slab drawn beneath it and broken off at each end." FIG. 1 brief: "The workpiece 50 is a flat panel drawn as a long horizontal slab under the suction cup 10." draft/numerals.md: "| 50 | workpiece |".
findings.fix: In the FIG. 2 brief change "a flat unnumbered slab" to "the workpiece 50", add the anchor "50 well inside the slab, clear of the suction cup" and add 50 to both the numeral table and the "Numerals shown on this figure" list.

structured_output.summary:
The candidate is a well-organised, internally coherent application whose prior-art discussion is, with two exceptions, faithful to the files in prior_art/ (US-10625955-B2, CN-110630621-B, US-10518985-B2, US-5310232-A, US-5374090-A, CN-2806399-Y, US-2024424646-A1, WO-2017156581-A1, WO-2022236379-A1 all check out against their quoted claims/abstracts). Its central recited relationship — the warning indicator activating at a warning vacuum reached before a release vacuum at which the cup ceases to retain the load — is a fair restatement in vacuum terms of the inventor's "The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped."

The problem is everything built around that core. The inventor's disclosure is nine sentences long and places only three things: the pump inside the rigid body, the lip on the cup, the handle on the body. The candidate nevertheless recites, in independent and dependent claims and supports in its own detailed description, a set of structures, placements, power connections and functional relationships the disclosure never states: pump-independent activation, the pump located close to the port with a consequently small evacuated volume, the indicator carried by and positioned on the rigid body, the battery powering the sensor and the indicator, and operation "without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body" — the last taken almost verbatim from the search wording in input/request.md, which expressly told the drafter to treat it "as a pointer to look in input/disclosure.md, never as text to import." The FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs add exactly the two artefacts input/request.md named as previously rejected: a duct between port and pump, and a sensing branch to the pressure sensor, together with a sensing location for the pressure sensor. Under the source-ledger rule these are all critical.

Note on scope of the figure review: figures/ contains only the four Markdown briefs. There are no rendered-*.png files and no review/figure-audit-evidence.json in this workspace, so no pixel, OCR, leader, hatch or cutting-plane verification was possible; the two mechanical failures you supplied are consistent with that. My figure findings are therefore against the brief text only, and I make no claim about rendered geometry.

findings.title: Pump-independent activation of the warning indicator is not in the inventor's disclosure
findings.detail: Three claims and two specification paragraphs recite that the indicator fires irrespective of whether the pump is running, and that it fires while the pump is still drawing air and losing ground to a leak. The inventor's disclosure says nothing whatever about the state of the pump at the moment of warning; it says only that the pump draws air through a port and that the indicator activates when vacuum is lost. This is an added functional relationship, and it is the relationship the conversation record shows the drafter selected as the sharpest distinction over the restart-threshold references — which is precisely why it needs a source and does not have one. The candidate's own detailed description cannot supply the support, because the candidate wrote it.
findings.evidence: Claim 2: "wherein the warning indicator is configured to activate at the warning vacuum whether or not the electric vacuum pump is operating." Claim 3: "...while the electric vacuum pump continues to draw air through the port and the vacuum continues to be lost." Detailed description ¶25: "If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the vacuum falls to the warning vacuum while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up." The whole of input/disclosure.md on the pump and the indicator is: "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum... The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: Cancel claims 2, 3 and 10 and renumber. Delete detailed-description ¶25 in full and delete the sentence in the summary beginning "In embodiments, the warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost whether or not the electric vacuum pump is running...". No other passage depends on them.

findings.title: Claim 8 and its supporting paragraph add a pump-to-port proximity, a small evacuated volume, and a resulting measurement behaviour
findings.detail: The disclosure states only that the pump is disposed inside the rigid body and draws air through a port. The candidate adds a positional relationship (pump close to the port), a consequent geometric property (the evacuated volume is short and small), and a consequent measurement result (a leak produces a fall prompt enough to be monitored rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir). Position, volume and the asserted sensing consequence are each untraced; the reservoir comparison is an engineering result the inventor never reports.
findings.evidence: Claim 8: "wherein the electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body close to the port, such that a volume from which air is drawn is short and small and a leak produces a fall in the vacuum that is monitored by the pressure sensor." Detailed description ¶29: "A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described above, because a leak of a given size then produces a fall in the vacuum that is prompt enough to be monitored by the pressure sensor 30 rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir." input/disclosure.md says only: "An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum."
findings.fix: Cancel claim 8 and renumber. Delete detailed-description ¶29 in full. The disclosed relationship ("disposed within the rigid body") already appears in claim 1 and in ¶9 and is unaffected.

findings.title: "Without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body" is imported search wording, not inventor disclosure
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 4 and 12; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶3 and ¶13; draft/06-summary.md ¶11
findings.detail: The inventor discloses a "cordless handheld vacuum lifter" and nothing more about external connections. The candidate converts that adjective into a recited negative limitation excluding a hose, a cord and an external controller, and asserts it four times. The wording tracks the search phrase quoted in input/request.md, which the drafter was told in terms not to import: "They are quoted in the SEARCH's words, not the inventor's: treat each as a pointer to look in input/disclosure.md, never as text to import." A hose exclusion and an external-controller exclusion are separate technical assertions from cordlessness and neither is disclosed.
findings.evidence: Claim 4: "...such that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter creates the vacuum, monitors the vacuum, and activates the warning indicator without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body." Claim 12: "...carrying the load with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body." Detailed description ¶3: "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14." input/request.md: "single-hand portable design with all components carried by rigid body without external hose or cord" ... "never as text to import." input/disclosure.md contains no reference to a hose, a cord or a controller.
findings.fix: Cancel claims 4 and 12 and renumber. In ¶3 delete the sentence beginning "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit..."; in ¶13 delete the final clause "and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use"; delete summary ¶11. The disclosed word "cordless" remains in the title, field and every claim preamble.

findings.title: The warning indicator's mounting and viewing position are recited and drawn but never disclosed
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 6 and 9; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶11; draft/06-summary.md ¶3 and ¶9; figures/FIG-1-SIDE-ELEVATION-LIFTER-IN-USE.md
findings.detail: The disclosure locates the pump ("inside the rigid body 14"), the lip (on the cup) and the handle (on the body), and locates nothing else. It never says the warning indicator is on or carried by the rigid body, still less that it is placed where a user gripping the handle can perceive it. "Carried by the rigid body" appears in independent claims 1 and 9, and the perceptibility limitation is claim 6. The FIG. 1 brief then fixes the placement on the sheet, which is geometry the text was widened to legitimise rather than the other way round.
findings.evidence: Claim 1: "a warning indicator carried by the rigid body and driven by the pressure sensor". Claim 6: "wherein the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle." Detailed description ¶11: "The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool." FIG. 1 brief: "The warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small discrete element on the outer surface of the upper side of the rigid body 14, beside the handle 16, facing upward toward the user." input/disclosure.md: "The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: In claims 1 and 9 delete "carried by the rigid body and" / "a warning indicator carried by the rigid body" so the indicator is recited exactly as disclosed ("a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor"). Cancel claim 6 and renumber. In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14..."; delete the corresponding sentence in summary ¶9 and the words "carried by the rigid body and" in summary ¶3. In the FIG. 1 brief, either drop 32 from the sheet or reduce the entry to "the warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small plain outline on the rigid body 14" with no facing, side or beside-the-handle statement.

findings.title: The battery is claimed as carried by the rigid body and as powering the pressure sensor and the warning indicator; the disclosure says only that it powers the pump
findings.where: draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 5, 9 and 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶11 and ¶33; draft/06-summary.md ¶3
findings.detail: The single disclosed sentence about the battery is "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." The candidate adds two things: a mounting ("carried by the rigid body", in both independent claims) and two further power connections to the sensor and the indicator, together with the consequence that monitoring and warning are available whenever the tool is in hand. Claims 5 and 14 recite the added connections outright.
findings.evidence: Claim 1: "a rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body and configured to power the electric vacuum pump." Claim 5: "wherein the rechargeable battery is further configured to power the pressure sensor and the warning indicator." Claim 14: "further comprising powering the pressure sensor and the warning indicator from the rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body while the load is retained." Detailed description ¶11: "The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand." input/disclosure.md: "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20."
findings.fix: Cancel claims 5 and 14 and renumber. In claims 1 and 9 delete "carried by the rigid body and" before "configured to power the electric vacuum pump". In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30..." and in ¶13 delete ", the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32" so the sentence reads "The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." In ¶33 delete ", the rechargeable battery 40 powering the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 throughout". In summary ¶3 delete "carried by the rigid body". Correspondingly delete the battery-to-sensor/indicator power lines from the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 briefs.

findings.title: FIG. 2 brief invents a duct between port and pump and a sensing location for the pressure sensor
findings.detail: The brief specifies a short duct with hatched walls running from the port to the pump, a flow arrow inside it, a path from beneath the cup into the body interior, and — most seriously — places the pressure sensor adjacent that duct. Where the sensor is plumbed is nowhere in the inventor's disclosure, which says only "A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum." input/request.md records this exact class of addition as having sunk an earlier round ("new structure: a suction passage, a sensing branch, a sealed region, each given a numeral and a location nobody disclosed") and imposes a hard rule against it: "introduce NO new numbered part, passage, region, port, chamber, surface or other structure". Being unnumbered does not make the duct any less a new passage, and the sensor's position beside it asserts a sensing point on the drawing.
findings.evidence: FIG. 2 brief: "The electric vacuum pump 20 is a block inside the interior cavity, on one side of the vertical centre line, positioned close to the port 22 and connected to it by a short duct drawn as a pair of hatched walls. An arrow inside that duct points from the port 22 toward the electric vacuum pump 20 to show the direction of air flow. The pressure sensor 30 is a smaller block inside the interior cavity, adjacent the duct between the port 22 and the electric vacuum pump 20." Also: "The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening through the wall of the suction cup 10 on the vertical centre line, giving a path from beneath the suction cup 10 into the interior of the rigid body 14."
findings.fix: Rewrite these three bullets to the disclosed facts only: "The electric vacuum pump 20 is a plain block inside the interior cavity of the rigid body 14. The pressure sensor 30 is a smaller plain block inside the interior cavity. The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening on the vertical centre line through which the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air." Delete the duct, its hatched walls, the flow arrow, the "positioned close to the port 22" phrase, the "path... into the interior of the rigid body 14" phrase and the "adjacent the duct" placement.

findings.title: FIG. 3 brief invents a pneumatic sensing branch to the pressure sensor
findings.detail: The schematic routes a branch of the port-to-pump pneumatic line to the pressure sensor block. That branch is a pneumatic connection and a sensing location, neither of which the inventor disclosed; the disclosure states only that the sensor monitors the grip vacuum and drives the indicator. This is the second of the two artefacts input/request.md names by name ("a sensing branch") as having caused an earlier round to be rejected.
findings.evidence: FIG. 3 brief: "The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening through the wall of the suction cup 10 and is connected by a plain pneumatic line running upward into the broken-line rectangle to the block of the electric vacuum pump 20... A branch of that pneumatic line runs to the block of the pressure sensor 30." input/disclosure.md: "A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum. The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost."
findings.fix: Delete the bullet "A branch of that pneumatic line runs to the block of the pressure sensor 30." Show the pressure sensor 30 as a plain block whose only drawn connection is the signal line to the warning indicator 32, which is the relationship the disclosure states.

findings.title: The sealing lip is given a peripheral position and a projecting form the disclosure does not state
findings.detail: The disclosure says only that the suction cup carries a flexible sealing lip. The candidate adds that the lip runs around the periphery of the cup, that it projects away from the rigid body, that it deflects and conforms on contact, and that it is the only part that touches the workpiece in normal use. Peripheral location and projection direction are structure; "the part... that touches the workpiece" is an exclusivity assertion. The figure briefs then place the lip "at the lower periphery of the suction cup 10" consistently with the added text.

When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use..." input/disclosure.md: "The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14."
findings.fix: Replace ¶7 with the disclosed statement and its immediate function: "The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face." In the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 briefs replace "at the lower periphery of the suction cup 10" with "on the suction cup 10, shown in contact with the upper face of the panel".

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suction plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried powered suction devices have likewise been described. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, a switch by which the pump is turned on and off, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, the sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across a resistor network fed by the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated there is the state of the power source and the sufficiency of the suction force for taking hold, not how much hold remains on an object already being carried.
12	
13	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed to the upper end of a suction cup body and a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, with a control unit connected between the pump and the power supply part, so that air is pumped out from between the suction cup body and the surface of a smooth material and is continuously pumped out after an airtight state has been reached in order to avoid loosening and falling during movement; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change, with a light source displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. Here again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep the pump running, and what the buzzer is tied to is a usage state rather than the amount of grip left.
14	
15	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure carrying a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure carrying a battery and an electric vacuum pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, and the lower part of the battery end carrying an air pressure sensor and a display screen which displays the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power, the battery being charged through a USB charging port [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device puts a number in front of the user and leaves the reading of the number, and the judgement of what it means for the panel in hand, to the user.
16	
17	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating a suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, a power storage unit, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, together with an attach indicator which the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator there reports that attachment has been achieved, being activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, and the response to a vacuum level below the preselected minimum is once more to run the pump.
18	
19	A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum, the passages of record describing that value only as a predetermined value.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither [REF:US-10625955-B2] nor [REF:CN-110630621-B] relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
26

1	This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.
2	
3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.
4	
5	The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.
6	
7	The warning vacuum is thus fixed by reference to the release vacuum, and not by reference to the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.
8	
9	In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.
10	
11	A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.
6	
7	The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.
12	
13	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.
14	
15	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
16	
17	The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.
18	
19	This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.
20	
21	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
22

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. When the user presses the activation key, the vacuum pump will act to pump out the air between the electric sucker and the component attached to the electric sucker, so that the electric sucker is adsorbed on the component. The pressure sensing unit can detect the pressure between the electric sucker and the component in real time. When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air between the electric suction cup and the component again. After the user sets up the electric chuck on the component that wants to adsorb, can make the electric chuck adsorb automatically on simply through pressing the start key on the component. Then, the electric suction cup can automatically detect the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component in real time, and automatically perform air suction again when the pressure is lower than a second preset pressure, so that the safety of related personnel using the electric suction cup can be ensured.

2

4	- Provenance: Ranked and read by the prior-art search for this project.
5	- Source: https://patents.google.com/patent/US5374090A/en
6	
7	## Why the search returned it
8	
9	Read in full (20,523 characters). Grounds 3 disclosed, 2 partial and 5 unconfirmed of 10 features, the rarest being warning indicator positioned on rigid body for visibility during lifting operation (paragraph p0010); rechargeable battery integrated into rigid body powering vacuum pump (paragraph p0009). Read as a whole it scores 90/100. Best disclosure found for: warning indicator remains active while grip vacuum persists below threshold; warning indicator positioned on rigid body for visibility during lifting operation.
10	
11	## Passages the search matched
12	
13	Abstract: A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers during the manufacture of integrated circuits. The wand device comprises a housing having a hollow interior and a tip for grasping objects. The tip is attached to the housing through a hollow tube, and has a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of an object to be grasped. The tip also has a recessed interior region having an air inlet therein. The wand device includes a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing. The vacuum pump produces a suction force at the air inlet on the tip. When the tip is placed against the surface of an object, the object is securely grasped due to the suction force exerted thereon by the wand tip. A switch located on the wand may be used to turn the vacuum pump on or off in order to grasp or release the object. Light-emitting diodes of different colors indicate to an operator whether or not the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object.
14	Claims: A cordless apparatus for grasping objects said apparatus comprising: a cordless housing having a first air inlet therein; means within said housing for creating a suction force at said first air inlet; means for applying said suction force to a surface of object to be grasped; and means for indicating to an operator whether said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object, said indicating means comprising: a first light-emitting diode which illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object; a second light-emitting diode which illuminates when said means for creating a suction force is activated and said suction force is not of sufficient strength to grasp said object; and means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force. The apparatus of claim 1 wherein the means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force includes: a power source disposed within said apparatus, said power source having a positive pole and a negative pole; a first resistor electrically connected between said positive pole of said power source and electrical ground; a second resistor connected in series with said first resistor; a third resistor connected in series with said first and second resistors; and an integrated circuit connected in parallel with said first, second, and third resistors, said integrated circuit detecting the voltage drop across each of said resistors, and causing said first light-emitting diode to illuminate when the total voltage drop exceeds a predetermined threshold, and causing said second light-emitting diode to illuminate when said total voltage drop is less than said predetermined threshold. A cordless wand device for grasping objects, said wand device comprising: a housing having a hollow interior: a tip for grasping objects, said tip being attached to said housing, and said tip having; a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against a surface of said object to be grasped; and a recessed interior region having a first air inlet therein; a power source positioned within said housing, said power source having a positive pole and a negative pole; a switch mounted on said housing; a vacuum pump for producing a suction force at a second air inlet, said vacuum pump positioned within said housing and electrically connected to said switch: said switch being electrically connected to said positive pole of said power source, whereby when said switch is closed, said vacuum pump is activated; a vacuum extension line disposed within said housing, said vacuum line comprising a hollow tube having a first and second end, the first end of said tube being attached to said second air inlet, and said second end extending through an aperture in a surface of said housing and connecting to said first air inlet of said tip of said wand device; and means for indicating to an operator whether said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object, said indicating means comprising: a first light-emitting diode which illuminates when said switch is closed and said suction force is of sufficient strength to grasp said object; a second light-emitting diode which illuminates when said switch is closed and said suction force is not of sufficient strength to grasp said object; and means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force. The cordless wand device of claim 3 wherein the means for determining the sufficiency of said suction force includes: a first resistor electrically connected between said positive pole of said power source and electrical ground; a second resistor connected in series with said first resistor; a third resistor connected in series with said first and second resistors; and an integrated circuit connected in parallel with said first, second, and third resistors, said integrated circuit detecting the voltage drop across each of said resistors, and causing said first light-emitting diode to illuminate when the total voltage drop exceeds a predetermined threshold, and causing said second light-emitting diode to illuminate when said total voltage drop is less than said predetermined threshold.
